newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Euro aluminium seen risking silicon supply squeeze.
newsitem.headline: Euro aluminium seen risking silicon supply squeeze.

text.p: Europe's aluminium industry will face a silicon metal supply shortfall unless the EU scraps anti-dumping duties and firms become more flexible in their purchasing, a Brazilian silicon exporter said on Wednesday.

"I believe there is a potential problem looming unless the aluminium industry in Europe changes its habits and its practices...There could be a real crisis within two to three years," Jack Green, European representative of Brasileira Carbureto de Calcio (CBCC), told a conference.

He forecast the European aluminium industry would need to purchase an additional 28,000 tonnes of silicon, or 20 percent of its total estimated requirements, by the turn of the century. Silicon is used to make primary and secondary aluminium, the latter for automotive components.

Russia, China and Brazil would have little problem providing the extra volume but they faced obstacles, Green said. Anti-dumping duties discouraged Chinese and Brazilian firms from exporting to the EU while quality concerns hampered Russian sales to European consumers.
Green called for an end to EU anti-dumping duties, which were introduced in 1992, and urged consumers not to be afraid of buying silicon that did not fit the "standard grade".

"To ensure that Europe can compete with Japan and the rest of the world for available supplies of silicon the first action must be to ensure that the EU eliminates all anti-dumping duties against China and Brazil forthwith," Green said.
Brussels announced last month it would review anti-dumping duties on Brazilian silicon imports.

"European aluminium consumers (also need) to show more flexibility in their buying habits. In other words buying departments should think of silicon in terms other than 'standard grade' silicon metal," Green continued.

Russia exported an estimated 55,000 tonnes of silicon in 1996 but the bulk ended up in the United States where consumers were more able to cope with the lower grade material, Green said. Only 5,000 tonnes of Russian silicon was sold into Europe.
Green warned that unless the European aluminium industry changed its buying habits, silicon producers would increasingly gear their business towards consumers in the chemical industry.

The aluminium industry was characterised by high sales and distribution costs, low growth and volatile conditions. Chemicals, in contrast, was a rapidly expanding market with fewer customers requiring larger shipments.

"The end result is that the silicon metal producers looking to maximise their financial return will by and large not consider the European aluminium industry as a priority end-use sector," Green said. -- Janet McBride, Vienna newsroom +43-1 531 12 254
